VCMalloc
A Virtually Contiguous
Memory Allocator
A custom allocator for Microsoft Windows that keeps user data virtually contiguous while the operating system retains full control of physical memory.

What VCMalloc delivers

A general-purpose allocator optimised for virtual contiguity, cache behaviour and low fragmentation.

Cache-aware gain on C = A x B naive multiplication (M up to 8,000).
The central result
MIMalloc already beats Malloc on speed, but pays up to 225% more memory. VCMalloc keeps Malloc-like memory consumption while matching or beating both on cycles — the only allocator in the comparison that produced perfectly contiguous allocations.

Motivation

Why contiguity is a performance problem

Perfectly adjacent structures eliminate fragmentation and improve both cache and program behaviour.
With perfect contiguity
  • Total fragmentation elimination — all structures adjacent
  • Fewer cache defects — prefetchers work on predictable spans
  • Better readability — layout mirrors the algorithm
  • GPU-ready — devices that require contiguity become usable
But adjacent blocks break resizing
  • Realloc and free move data — time-consuming
  • Every trailing reference must be updated — linear cost
  • Pre-allocating large blocks instead is wasteful — sizing is guesswork and memory is stranded
The design tension
Contiguity gives locality but forbids the one operation data structures need most. Existing contiguous allocators (CMA, GCMA) sidestep this by being static — all in-kernel, all fixed size. VCMalloc has to keep contiguity while resizing.
VCMalloc  ·  Motivation3 / 16
Core idea

Virtual contiguity without physical contiguity

The application sees one gap-free address range. The operating system still scatters the backing frames.
Conventional allocator
User pointers land wherever the heap allows
VIRTUAL ADDRESS SPACE
Data structures are dispersed across the heap
PHYSICAL MEMORY
Frames interleaved with unrelated data
VCMalloc
One hypercontainer, many containers, still physically scattered
Containers are adjacent and in order
PHYSICAL MEMORY
Frames still scattered — contiguity is virtual only
VCMalloc is deliberately not a drop-in malloc: the hypercontainer argument changes the call signature, so the user opts in and keeps explicit control of layout.

Mechanism

What actually happens on each operation

Five steps, driven by the Windows AWE API rather than the ordinary heap.
1
Reserve
vc_hcalloc
Pick an address after the last hypercontainer, stepping by system allocation granularity until one is free. No physical memory is committed yet.
2
Allocate
vc_malloc
Create a container inside a chosen hypercontainer, request page frames from the OS and map them into the container's virtual range.
3
Resize
vc_resize
Release or request pages inside the hypercontainer and revise offsets. Guest bytes copied are always smaller than one page.
4
Reallocate
vc_realloc
If the container cannot grow in place, move it to the end of the hypercontainer by remapping zones rather than copying data.
5
Release
vc_hcfree
Unmap and free the frames, return the virtual range, then update the manager.
Windows AWE API
The foundation
VirtualAllocAllocateUserPhysicalPagesMapUserPhysicalPagesFreeUserPhysicalPages
Meta-information itself is heap-allocated and grows implicitly — so VCMalloc offers APIs to pre-extend contexts and avoid repeated reallocation.
VCMalloc  ·  Mechanism6 / 16
Contiguity under change

Three ways to reallocate

Each strategy trades a different cost: preserving order, avoiding fragmentation, or resizing many arrays at once.
In order
vc_resize
Keeps the allocation order intact, so the data structure stays linear. Containers after the resized one are shifted to hold their positions. The pointer never changes.
Preserves order
Shifts trailing containers
Out of order
vc_realloc
Only the affected container moves, and only when it cannot grow in place — it is relocated to the end of the hypercontainer. Cheaper, but leaves fragmentation between 0 and SP-1 bytes.
Touches one container
Residual fragmentation
Multiple
vc_mresize
Resizes s consecutive containers in a single remapping pass — the right choice when a multi-dimensional array grows, since all dimensions resize together.
One remap for M rows
Ideal for ND arrays
Fragmentation bound
F = SP − Smod  when SΔ > 0
F = Smod  otherwise
Worst case is one page short of full. Guest bytes copied are always smaller than one page, which is what keeps reallocation cheap compared with the traditional copy-everything approach.

Interface

The VCMalloc API surface

Seven entry points across three families — roughly 1,500 lines of C and C++.
Allocation 4 calls
vc_hcalloc(s) Pre-allocate a virtual hypercontainer of size s
vc_malloc(hc, s) Allocate s bytes in hypercontainer hc
vcr_malloc(hc, ref, s) As above, and track a user reference
vca_malloc(s) Allocate s bytes and track a reference
Reallocation 3 calls
vc_resize(ptr, s) Resize a container in place to s bytes
vc_mresize(ptr, sizes, s) Resize s consecutive containers in one pass
vc_realloc(ptr, s) Resize in place, or move the container to the end of hc
Deallocation 2 calls
vc_hcfree(hc) Deallocate an entire hypercontainer
vc_hcmfree(hcm) Free every hypercontainer in the manager
Typical use
char* hc = vc_hcalloc(hc_size);
double** A = vc_malloc(hc,
sizeof(double*)*M);
for (i = 0; i < M; i++)
A[i] = vc_malloc(hc,
sizeof(double)*M);
vc_hcfree(hc);
No concurrency yet
The current version has no concurrent allocation strategy. Multi-threaded users must add their own synchronisation.
4 KB page size chosen deliberately over 2 MB large pages, to avoid early reservation and system-wide fragmentation.

Synthesis

The trade-off, in one picture

Fragmentation against memory footprint, across all three structure sizes. The lower-left corner is ideal.
Memory footprint vs. average fragmentation
Each point is one allocator at one matrix size
MIMalloc
Low fragmentation, but up to 225% more memory. Fast, and expensive.
Malloc
Reasonable memory, but the worst fragmentation — up to 792 MiB average.
VCMalloc
Malloc-like memory with near-zero fragmentation. The balanced option.
VCMalloc does not win every single row. Its advantage is that it is the only allocator that is never the worst choice on either axis.

Limitations

What VCMalloc does not do yet

The results are strong, but the design carries real costs that a production deployment must weigh.
No concurrency
The current version implements no concurrent allocation strategy. Multi-threaded applications must add their own synchronisation.
Not a drop-in malloc
The hypercontainer argument changes the call signature, so existing source must be adapted. On large codebases this is slow and error-prone.
Page size is 4 KB
Large 2 MB pages would cut TLB pressure, but must be reserved at boot. VCMalloc trades TLB efficiency for predictable fragmentation.
Evaluation is narrow
Results come from micro-benchmarks, matrix multiplication and three SPEC CPU 2017 applications on one Windows 11 workstation.
Adopting VCMalloc is a deliberate trade: you give up a transparent malloc interface and gain an explicit, user-controlled memory layout. That suits workloads — imaging, vision, linear algebra — where contiguity is worth the integration cost.
VCMalloc  ·  Limitations14 / 16
Outlook

Where VCMalloc goes next

The authors point to four concrete extensions of the current design.
Other operating systems
Port the allocator beyond Windows, where the AWE API is specific to this platform.
Physically contiguous backing
Combine virtual contiguity with a physically contiguous allocator such as GCMA, removing the last remapping step.
Irregular data structures
Design layouts for non-rectangular structures — graphs, sparse matrices, trees — that fit the container model.
GPGPU workloads
Extend the techniques to GPU memory, where contiguity is already a hard requirement.
Open source and reusable today
About 1,500 lines of C and C++. Compile it as an object file or link it as a library.
